Quo utroque loco Sixt. interpres, Et caedent cervicem vitulae in valle, et lavabunt manus super caput vitulae excervicatae : quod non putem ex fide interpretis ; alioqui proferendus auctor, aut probatus grammaticus, cui τὸ, νευροκοπεῖν, sit ipsum τενοκοπεῖν · non suffragines nervosque succidere, relicto vivo jumento, cui sic illa succiderentur, sed quasi inutili ; quod praesertim in equis saepius factitatum (Dei etiam quandoque jussu) habet Scriptura, sed cervicem cedere, decollare, et, ut nostri Pagn. et Malven., decervicare. Sic quidem Hebr. et qui ex illis reddunt, nec non Vulg. caedent in ea cervices vitulae : verum aliud est Hebraea, ut nunc habent, ac communiter reddi solent, interpretando reddere ; aliud τὰ τῶν LXX Seniorum Latine repraesentare. Legerintne sapientissimi viri, quod nunc est in Hebr. [...], quod sic reliqui interpretantur, caput demere, cervicem incidere ; Arab. mactare seu jugulare ; Syriac. decollare ; Samarit. decervicare ; Pagn. et Malv. in eo tamen intellexerint aliud significari, habuerintque ex traditione apud eos vigente ; nempe non justum hoc sacrificium, et quo vere vitula immolaretur, quasi expiando homicidio sic occulto, sed quamdam quasi mali averruncationem, debilitata solummodo vitula, longeque amandata in regionem desertam, quo se immunes ab homicidii scelere vicini incolae profiterentur ; vel aliam huic affinem vocem habuerint, ipsam nimirum, quae sic ab iisdem redditur Jos. II, 6, Τοὺς ἵππους αὐτῷ νευροκοπήσει ; [...], perindeque II Reg. VIII, 4 ; et I Paral. XVIII, 4, quibus duobus locis οἱ LXX sensum, non verba reddiderunt, Παρέλυσε τὰ ἅρματα · Dissolvit currus ; nempe quod subnernavit omnes eorum equos et subjugales, uti Vulg. expressit ; alii viderint. Unum mihi certum, sic eos sensisse, huncque verum ejus loci sensum opinatos esse ; nempe, sicut caper seu hircus, ipse devotus, in solitudinem unus emittebatur, altero immolato Domino : sic in desertum (terram scilicet incultam, qualis ibi describitur) emissam et vitulam seu vaccam, ubi quaedam in ea quasi immolatio in subnervatione seu debilitatione praecesserat, manuumque lotio super caput ejus, sic subnervatae, seu aliae devotiones, quibus ipsa in se scelus recepisse, longeque asportare significabatur, expressiore scilicet Domini Jesu figura ; qui sic vulneratus, propter scelera nostra, illisque in se receptis, in aeternum vivit in regione deserta ; gentium scilicet Ecclesia, quae deserta erat, et non pariebat, nuncque plures filios habet, quam quae virum habeat (Judaea scilicet) uti habet Isaias. Sic alte contemplatus in Glaphyr. Cyril. qui et Maximo praeiverit. Sic itaque ille (ut ex multis pauca ejus referam) : Ὅρα τὴν δάμαλιν, εἰς τραχεῖαν καὶ ἀνήροτον ἀποφερομένην φάραγγα. Μετὰ γάρ τοι τὸν τίμιον σταυρὸν, ὅτε τραυματίας ηὕρηται Χριστός, τῆς Ἰουδαίων ἀποπεφοίτηκε γῆς · μεταπεφοίτηκε δὲ λοιπὸν ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν χώραν, ἥτις οὐκ εἴργασται, οὐδὲ σπείρεται · Vide vitulam in vallem asperam et incultam deductam. Nam post venerandam crucem, quando vulneratus inventus est Christus, discessit a terra Judaeorum, migravitque in regionem gentium, quae nunquam culta fuerot, neque sementem acceperat. Postque alia : Ἐκεῖ διὰ τῶν θείων ἱερουργῶν νευροκοπεῖσθαι δεῖν ἔφη τὴν δάμαλιν. Τελεῖται γὰρ παρ' ἡμῖν τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν τὸ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον · καὶ ὁμολογοῦντες αὐτοῦ τὸ πάθος καὶ τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνάβιωσιν, ταῖς μυστικαῖς πρόσεσμεν εὐλογίαις. Τοῦτο γάρ, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ νευροκοπεῖσθαι τὴν δάμαλιν. Καταγγέλλοντες γὰρ τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὡσαύτως καὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν, τὸ σεπτὸν τελοῦμεν μυστήριον. Nempe a crucis immolatione, ad symbolicam in Eucharistia, ipsam immolationem, sic tamen ut semper in ea, viva hostia sit, ejus mysterii devotissimus cultor Cyrillus, transiens : Ibi vitulae nervi concidendi, per divinos sacerdotes. Christi enim mysterium apud nos, qui ex gentibus sumus, peragitur ; ejusque passionem, ac ex mortuis resurrectionem annuntiantes, ad mysticas eulogias accedimus. Id enim puto est, quod vitulae nervi concidantur : quod scilicet, annuntiantes mortem ipsius, atque item resurrectionem, venerandum mysterium peragimus. Equos hostium tum primum Deus subnervandos jussit, cum eorum atque curruum magno apparatu in Hebraeos pugnarunt ; quo docerentur, non in eis, sed in Deo adjutore, qui horum victores reddidisset, ponendam esse fiduciam. Sic Rab. Chim. Jos. II. De bobus eorumque subnervatione, etsi non ita familiare ac de equis in Scriptura, exstat tamen illustre exemplum Genes. XLIX, 6, in benedictione Simeonis et Levi. [...] Subnervaverunt bovem, Seniores οἱ LXX, Ἐνευροκόπησαν ταῦρον, quod vox illa perinde ac murum significat, cum alia aliaque motione, quae tunc nulla scriptae legebantur, sed corde tenebantur : eodem modo Samarit. alii et Vulg. murum ; quod non ita cohaerere videtur : In furore suo occiderunt virum, et in animositate sua, suffoderunt murum. Nisi quis metaphorice accipiat, uti Menoch., ut significentur Hemor et Sichem urbis principes, qui illi pro muro erant. Sed hoc remotius. Virum quis existimare possit ipsum Hemor ; bovem seu taurum, ejus filium Sichem, sic tauri in morem libidinis impotentem, qua et totius ejus tragoediae auctor fuit ; nisi quod ille non subnervatus, sed una cum patre necatus aperte dicitur Gen. XXXIV, quae duo haud videantur οἱ LXX tanto vocum abusu, confudisse. Ut ergo in homine, totam civitatem plebemque et principes sic occisos intellexit Jacobus, sic in bove, quidquid gregum armentorumque erat, quae omnia illos vastasse ait sacer textus Gen. XXXIV. Sic ergo in eis, alia sustulerint, alia subnervarint, ne princeps usui essent, ipsorumque furoris ex spectaculo in posterum monumentum forent. Sic ipsa valde pudenda, jactat irae impotens furor quasi magnifica.

en: (Continuing the note on 'hamstrung', Deut. 21:6.) The Latin translator renders both places 'they shall cut the neck of the heifer'; the editor doubts this is faithful, since the Greek verb for hamstringing is not 'to cut the neck'. The Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Samaritan and Latin versions give 'behead', 'slay' or 'decapitate', but the Septuagint rendering is something else: the heifer was not truly sacrificed to expiate a hidden murder, but crippled and sent into a desert region, so that the neighbours could declare themselves free of the crime. The same verb is used of horses at Josh. 11:6, 2 Sam. 8:4 and 1 Chron. 18:4, where the Septuagint gives the sense, 'he loosed the chariots', that is, he hamstrung the horses. As the goat was sent alone into the wilderness while the other was offered to the Lord, so the crippled heifer sent into the desert prefigures the Lord Jesus, wounded for our sins and living for ever in the deserted land, the Church of the gentiles, who has more children than she who has a husband (Isaiah). Cyril in his Glaphyra anticipated Maximus: after the cross Christ left the land of the Jews for the nations, and the hamstringing of the heifer by the priests is the mystery of Christ celebrated among the gentiles, proclaiming his death and resurrection. God ordered the enemy's horses hamstrung so that Israel would trust not in them but in God. The same verb occurs at Gen. 49:6 in the blessing of Simeon and Levi, 'they hamstrung an ox', which the Septuagint took with the sense of 'wall'; the editor weighs whether the ox is Hamor's son Sichem, and concludes that the text speaks of the whole city, its flocks and herds, laid waste as a lasting memorial of their rage.

text: (o) Τεσσαράκοντα δηλοῦντος τὰ αἰσθητά. Videantur haec περιττότερον dicta, nec satis ex lege exactae allegoriae. Ut enim August. in Joan. V, quadragenarius numerus in quadam perfectione accipi solet, eaque ratione in jejunio consecratus est : nec materia et forma aliud sunt quam ipsa sensilia, in quibus proinde non videtur debuisse Maximus duo quaerere supra quadraginta, siquidem quadraginta (ob quatuor scilicet elementa) exponit τὰ αἰσθητά, quasi ex illis coalita : nisi forte hoc libuit ludere in allegoriae campo, quod alia aliis immediatus ad ipsa se habeant, possitque animus distinctionis aliquid cogitare inter illa.
anchorLine: δηλοῦντος τὰ αἰσθητά (ο) · ὕλη δὲ καὶ τὸ εἶδος προσ-
en: 'Forty signifying sensible things': this seems said to excess and not quite by the rule of strict allegory. For, as Augustine says on John 5, forty is usually taken for a kind of perfection, and for that reason was consecrated in fasting. Matter and form are nothing other than the sensible things themselves, so Maximus seems not to have needed to look for two beyond forty, since he explains forty (from the four elements) as the sensible things, as if compounded of them. Unless perhaps he chose to play in the field of allegory, because some things stand more directly to those things themselves, and the mind may think of some distinction among them.

Vocem [...] accepit Maximus, ut est ἀπὸ τοῦ [...] quinque punctorum, quod est, sagena, plagae, rete ; haec enim ferarum ἀποστροφή, seu bestiarum, sive quod haec fugiant studeantque cavere, sive quod incauta animalia se in illa, esca scilicet illecta, conjiciant, juxta utramque ejus vocis significationem, etsi contrariam. Quod vero ratione Jordanis inde orientis, gratiam sacri baptismatis significare ait Maximus, contrario sensu accipiendum anathema, ut qui illo capiuntur Dei ἀνάθημα sint, et ad vitam capiantur.

en: 'Thyris' is rendered 'window'; the Hebrew word for 'looked' is Chaldaic for window, and its plural is 'windows' (Dan. 6:11). The derivation of Cana is known: from the Hebrew for 'possessed'. For Galilee the editor cannot believe Maximus wrote 'apokalypsis', revelation, rather than 'apokylisis', revolution (rolling), since that word is known to sound from the Hebrew; a careful writer would not stray so far on so common a point. A copyist could easily err from similar-sounding words, as some Latins wrote 'revelation' for 'revolution'. Suidas has Galilee as 'rolled down'. Maximus did not explain Hermon from its Hebrew root but from the man's character: 'anxious, troubled, fisher', which fits a harmful and treacherous man. Maximus took the other name as 'cherem', net or snare, from which wild beasts flee or into which they are lured, so that they are destroyed, devoted to human use, which is the first meaning of the Hebrew word. His claim that the Jordan rising there signifies baptismal grace is to be taken in the contrary sense of 'anathema', that those caught by it become God's anathema and are caught for life.

text: (i) Ὁ Κάϊν. Vocis Cain, non aliud quaerendum etymum quam quod ipsa Eva assignavit, eo illi nomine indito, Gen. IV, quod scilicet virum nacta esset ; filio scilicet aucta velut possessione ; quod nihil facit ad prudentiam carnis : quam ipsam Maximus non in ejus nominis etymo spectaverit, sed in ipsius moribus atque indole, et quod fratrem, justum Abelem oppresserit, uti prudentia carnis opprimit sensum mentis. Abel, vanitatem sonat, quasi rem nihili ; cujus sensus maxime ad poenitentiam conducit ; quod se nimirum vere quis agnoscat, ac quod nihili est, ipsa hominis ratione, longeque eo aliquid minus, peccatoris ascita conditione.
anchorLine: Ὁ Κάϊν (i) λαμβάνεται ἐπὶ τοῦ φρονήματος τῆς
en: For the name Cain no etymology need be sought beyond the one Eve gave it (Gen. 4), that she had gained a man, her son being as it were a possession. That has nothing to do with the prudence of the flesh. Maximus saw that prudence not in the etymology of the name but in Cain's character, and in his oppressing his just brother Abel, as the prudence of the flesh oppresses the mind's sense. Abel means vanity, as if a thing of nothing. This sense leads especially to repentance, when a man truly recognizes himself as nothing, and even less than nothing by the sinner's acquired condition.

text: (j) Καὶ περιγράφεται. Quasi certis terminis finitur ; quod quasi inconveniens habere videtur Maximus ; forte ob loca Scripturae, quibus ejus quaedam immensitas, omnem numerum vincens, describitur. Exponit itaque circumscribi Dei misericordiam, penes eorum capacitatem, qui illius effectus suscipiunt ; pro quorum ratione sunt illa ejus pondera, quod Dei dona non ἄκριτα sint ; quae scilicet ipse a se temere nullaque justa ratione mortalibus conferat, non pro cujusque (praeeunte gratia) operis merito ac cooperatione.
anchorLine: γράφεται (j), εἰκότως. Μᾶλλον οὖν τοῦτο χρὴ ὑπο-
en: 'And is circumscribed': as if bounded by fixed limits, which Maximus seems to find unfitting, perhaps because of Scripture passages that describe an immensity of his mercy beyond all number. So he explains that God's mercy is circumscribed in proportion to the capacity of those who receive its effects. That is why his gifts are weighed: they are not indiscriminate, but are not given by God at random or without just reason, and not according to each person's merit and cooperation (with grace going before).

III, 8, de lectulo Salomonis, ambiente armato fortissimo milite, gladiis accincto, ἀπὸ θάμβους ἐν νυξί · a pavore in noctibus ; et ut Sym. διὰ φόβους νυκτερινούς, propter timores nocturnos ; quomodo Vulg. habet, meminitque Theodoret. Pauperi mitique ipsa paupertas morumque lenitas armis omnibus potentior ad eos depellendos timores, et ut placide a diurnis quiescat laboribus prorsusque reficiatur.
anchorLine: Τί ἐστιν, « Ὅπλον ἐν φόβοις νυκτερινοῖς (k),
en: This passage is surely from Proverbs, by another reading, though it does not occur there. Almost twin to it is Cant. 3:8 on Solomon's bed, ringed by a strong armed soldier with sword at his side, 'because of fear in the nights'; so Symmachus has 'because of night terrors', as the Vulgate reads and Theodoret recalls. For the poor and gentle man, poverty and mildness of character are stronger than all weapons for driving off those fears, so that he may rest quietly from the day's labours and be wholly restored.

text: (l) Ἀντισηκούμενόν τι παροδικόν. Altam Maximi sententiam ut elicerem, necesse habui, ut quod Antiquarius errore asperserat, emendarem : ἀντὶ τοῦ, παράδικον, τὸ, παροδικόν · ἀντὶ τοῦ, πονηρῷ, τὸ, μονίμῳ. Liquet enim bonas cogitationes alias aliis conferri ; quarum aliae judicii confessionem ex examine habeant, aliae plena bonitate et explorata, laudis confessionem ac jucunditatem. Accepit ergo Maximus τὸ ἐγκατάλειμμα ἐνθυμίου, pro cogitatione tenacius animo haerente, inque illo relicta ac quasi habitu perseverante, per cujus oppositionem dictum sit τὸ ἐνθύμιον, cogitatio quomodocunque, ipsa volatica et fugax, in qua ipsa reus sit animus, quod non coluerit, sed velut semen in via, sibi facile abripi seu avolare passus sit. Maximi expositioni valde affinis Athanasii : Ἐγκατάλειμμα ἐνθυμίου, ὁ κεκαθαρευμένος ἐστὶ λογισμὸς κατ' ἐκλογὴν χάριτος · Reliquiae cogitationis, emundata cogitatio sunt, secundum gratiae delectum ; quam sic mundam in judicio inventam, mox participem futuram ait divinae festivitatis seu jucunditatis. Euseb. quoque, Τὸ δὲ ἐνθύμιον καθαρόν, ἁμαρτίας ὃν ἐγκατάλειμμα, ἑορτάζει · Pura cogitatio, quam deficiat peccatum, haec festum aget, seu jucundabitur. Sic enim vult Euseb. non quod absone edidit, reddiditque Cord. Cogitationis autem a peccato puritas, cum de reliquiis sit, festum agit. Sequiturque idem Euseb. ἢ καὶ τὸ ἀπηλεῖφθαι τὸ περὶ τούτου ἀμφίβολον, ἀναδειχθείσης ἐν αὐτῷ καθαρότητος, ἐφ' ᾗ ὁ ἅγιος ἑορτάζει · Vel quod jam nulla relicta de ipsa ambiguitas sit, declarata, qua nitet, munditia, ob quam sanctus festum agit gaudioque exsultat. Est ergo utrique interpr. ἐγκατάλειμμα τοῦ ἐνθυμίου, relictae a judicio probatae, electae, mundae cogitationes, nihil jam incerti habentes, eoque animi gaudium festumque impedientes ; Maximo autem, eaedem animo firmiter manentes atque perfectae ; quod totum parturiit vox illa τῶν LXX, ἐγκατάλειμμα, aliaque plura in paraphrasi, quae nolim referre. Hebraea longe videntur distare : habent enim [...], redduntque Residuum irarum accinges : seu etiam cinges ac ligabis, quod est, impedies, ut exponit Rab. D. in libro Radicum : a quo longe abest Paraph. Chald. At in reliquos populos arma furoris apparabis : vel ut alius, Residuum furoris, quod remansit tibi ab ira, qua iratus fuisti, praeparabis ad dispergendas gentes. Hier. : Reliquiis irae accingeris. Habuerunt oi LXX cum [...] loco [...] ex qua litterae permutatione tanta haec diversitas orta est : nec forte τὸ ἐνθυμίον, aliter acceperint, quam ἀπὸ τοῦ, θυμός, quod est ira, furor, excandescentia ; irae fervor et calor, ut sonant Hebraica. Erant certe viri Hebraica, quam Graeca doctiores ; suntque non raro alias secuti vocum significationes, quam quae apud probatos auctores nobis relictos habentur. Cum ergo θυμός et pro animo et pro ira accipiatur, potuerunt illi ad alteram significationem respicere, in illa voce ἐνθύμιον. Sic Arist. VII Polit. c. 7, τὸ, ἔνθυμος exponit θυμοειδής, qua voce Graeci iram ipsamque irascendi vim, passim vocitant ; vixque animosum magnosque spiritus habentem intelligas, quin illi irarum vis comes sit, quae ipsa illos animos fulciat. en: To bring out Maximus's deep meaning the editor had to correct what the old editor had spoiled by mistake: for 'paradikon' read 'parodikon', and for 'wicked' read 'abiding'. Good thoughts are plainly granted in different ways: some bear a confession of judgment after testing, others, wholly good and proven, a confession of praise and joy. So Maximus took 'the remnant of the thought' for a thought held more firmly in the mind and left there as a settled habit, as against the mere passing and fleeting thought, for which the mind is to blame because it did not cultivate it but let it be snatched away like seed on the road. Athanasius is very close: the remnant of a thought is the purified thought, by the choice of grace; and Eusebius too says the pure thought, of which sin is the remnant, keeps the feast, and adds that the doubt about it is wiped out. So both interpreters mean thoughts left behind after judgment, approved and pure, with nothing uncertain, while Maximus means the same thoughts firmly settled and perfect. The Hebrew seems to differ widely: it gives 'the remnant of wrath you will gird on', or 'you will bind'; Jerome has 'you will be girded with the remnants of wrath'. The Septuagint read one letter for another, hence the large difference; they may have taken 'enthymion' from 'thymos', anger, since the Hebrew sense is the heat of wrath. 'Thymos' means both spirit and anger, so they could have had the second meaning in view, as Aristotle's Politics 7 glosses 'enthymos' as spirited. The remnant of thought or of anger is in plainer sense one and the same, but the first with a diminishing particle. (The note breaks off at the foot of the page.)

text: (m) Μαργοῦ λεγομένου. Perinde Etymolog. iisdem pene verbis, vel ipse a Maximo mutuatus, vel ambo ab aliquo superiore, qui et fucum fecerit. Res certe extra omnem fidem, ac cujus Aristoteles, perinde ac alii, nihil meminerit : cum alioqui clara sit vocis etymologia, nihilque doctos utravis pars ejus compositionis lateat, τὸ, γαστήρ, et τὸ, μάργος. Suid. Μάργης καὶ μάργος, μαινόμενος · καὶ ὑπερμαργότερος, ὁ ὑπερμαινόμενος · καὶ γαστρίμαργος, ὁ περὶ τὴν γαστέρα μεμηνώς. Port. Qui circum ventrem insanit. Insane ventris replendi cupiditati deditus. Num et Aristoteli obrepserit, ut ista fabulosa de animalculo hoc scripserit, vel alii confixerint illique ascripserint quae ita forsitan simplicitate et mendacio, uti de Phoenice ave ostendunt eruditi, ipseque Maximus Epist. ad Petrum illustrem, ubi serio magis dogmata tradit, credita sint, alii viderint. Mihi non displicet sic opinari ; eoque vulgi arrepto commento, in eo Maximum non spernendam tropologiam instituisse.
anchorLine: μαργοῦ λεγομένου (m), ὅπερ γεννᾶται ἀπὸ σήψεως,
en: The Etymologicum has almost the same words, either borrowing from Maximus or both from some earlier source that also added the gloss. The matter is certainly beyond belief, and Aristotle and others say nothing of it, though the etymology is clear and neither part of the compound, 'gaster' (belly) and 'margos' (mad), is hidden from the learned. Suidas: 'margos' means raving, 'gastrimargos' means mad about the belly; Portus: one frantic about his belly. Whether this fabulous tale about the little creature crept in on Aristotle, or others forged it and ascribed it to him, perhaps in simplicity and falsehood, as scholars show of the Phoenix bird, and as Maximus himself believed in his letter to Peter the Illustrious, where he treats doctrine more seriously, others may judge. The editor is content to think so: Maximus took up the popular story and built on it a tropology not to be despised.
